tasks.task_description: Subtask 1: Interpret the public-report data and assess whether the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time can be predicted, and with what precision. Scope: all 4,440 reports (14 Positive ID, 2,069 Negative ID, 2,342 Unverified, 15 Unprocessed), Aug 2019 - Dec 2020, Washington State. Goal: a defensible statement about the spatial-temporal pattern of confirmed detections and the uncertainty around it.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) Lab Status 'Positive ID' is ground truth for V. mandarinia (state entomology lab); (b) confirmed reports are NOT an independent Poisson process - a newly introduced colony spreads slowly from a founding nest, queens disperse on the order of tens of km, workers forage within a few km, so confirmed detections arrive in spatial and temporal bursts around a few actual colonies; (c) scattered background reports elsewhere are mostly mistaken sightings, for which independence is roughly acceptable (checked below); (d) queen-range radius R = 30 km (problem statement) is the dispersion scale. Parameter table (empirical inputs): R = 30 km, interval [20, 40] km, source: problem statement (estimated range of a new queen); colony-era split (2019 founding vs 2020 activity), source: the dataset's own confirmed-report dates (Subtask 1 result). Method: cluster-based spatial analysis of the 14 confirmed reports (two colony eras: 2019 founding, 2020 activity) with nearest-neighbor distances and a 30 km range ring, plus a formal independence check (quadrant-occupancy test against the binomial null) on the 2,032 negative reports of 2020, where independence is assumed to hold. This is sound because it tests the independence assumption where it is expected to hold, and refuses it where the biology says it fails, instead of applying one generative model to everything.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cluster/spread model. Let P = {(x_i, t_i)} be the 14 confirmed reports, coordinates in km (equirectangular projection at mean latitude 48.9 deg: x = (lon + 122.5)*111.32*cos(lat0), y = lat*110.57). Statistics: pairwise distance matrix D via pdist; nearest-neighbor distribution; fraction within the queen-range ring f = |{i in P_2020: min_j in P_2019 ||p_i - p_j|| <= R}| / |P_2020| with R = 30 km, and Wilson score 95% CI for f. Independence diagnostic for the background N (2,032 negative reports of 2020): split the study region at the median latitude/longitude into 4 quadrants, counts (n_1..n_4) tested against Binomial(n, 1/4) per quadrant. Precision of the spread prediction is the CI width of f and the nearest-neighbor distance spread. Data cleaning (applied before modelling): 4,440 rows, no duplicate GlobalID; 72 unparseable detection dates (8 Excel serial-0 '12/30/1899', 3 '<Null>', 5 out-of-range years 515/1200/1600/1980) set to missing and flagged by a month_missing feature; Lab Comments whitespace-only treated as missing; the 29-column attachment feature block (n_files, n_images, n_video, has_pdf, has_zip, has_doc) joined from the 3,305-row image manifest on GlobalID (2,127 reports have >= 1 file).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: all 14 confirmed reports lie in western Washington (lat 48.78-49.15, lon -123.94 to -122.42); median pairwise distance 9.7 km (min 0.01, max 118.7). Temporal: 5 confirmations Sep-Dec 2019 (founding window), 9 in 2020 (May, Jun, Aug, Sep x4, Oct). All 9 of the 2020 confirmations fall within 30 km of the 2019 core: f = 1.0, Wilson 95% CI [0.701, 1.0]; median distance from a 2020 confirmation to the nearest 2019 confirmation 8.3 km (max 29.8 km). Quadrant test on the 2020 negatives: counts 528/528/488/488 of 2,032, p = 0.318 vs the independent null - not rejected, consistent with the background being a roughly homogeneous mistaken-sighting rate. Interpretation: the spread over the 15-month observation window is predictably local - confined to the founding area within the 30 km queen range, with no statistically supported evidence of spread beyond it; precision is limited by the small count (n = 14), so the honest statement is 'all observed spread is within 30 km of the founding cluster, and the 95% lower confidence bound on the fraction of new colonies within range is 0.70'. Limitations/biases: n = 14 is tiny; confirmation is conditional on public reporting and lab verification, so unreported colonies are invisible (the model predicts spread of *reported* positives, not of true colonies); the 118.7 km outlier pair is a single far report (Bellingham-area, 2019-09-19) that could be a mislabeled or a genuinely independent second introduction - the cluster statistic is robust to it (still 9/9 within 30 km).

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2: Using only the supplied dataset (report text, dates, coordinates, attachment manifest), build, analyze and discuss a model that predicts the likelihood that a report is a mistaken classification (i.e. not V. mandarinia). Scope: 2,083 labeled reports as training; the model must output a per-report probability of being a true positive.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the labeling process is media-gated - lab verification requires a photo or specimen, and 98.6% of labeled reports carry a file vs 2.9% of Unverified reports (expert exchange 1: missing media/dates track reporter diligence and channel, not the insect), so the classifier is fit on the lab-verifiable subpopulation and its output is P(true positive | report is lab-verifiable); (b) note text, date, location and attachment features carry the signal; (c) the 14 positives are all genuine (lab-confirmed). Method: logistic regression (L2-regularized, C = 1) with class weighting to handle the 14:2,069 imbalance, trained with stratified 5-fold cross-validation so every in-sample probability is an out-of-fold estimate; features are 23 deterministic regex indicators from the Notes field, note length, 29 attachment features from the image manifest, and 6 time features (month flags 2019/2020/missing, submission lag). Regularization (C = 1) and 5-fold CV are the robustness measures against the severe imbalance and the small positive class; a naive baseline P = 14/2083 = 0.0067 is the comparison. Goodness of fit: CV AUC, top-k capture of the 14 positives, and score-separation statistics with Wilson intervals.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: p_i = P(y_i = 1 | x_i) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(beta_0 + beta' x_i))), y = 1 for Positive ID, 0 for Negative ID. Design matrix x_i has 35 features: size words (huge/giant/enormous/large), big, yellow, black, sting, nest, many/swarm/flock, swarm, dead, killed/brought-in, brought (jar/pot/specimen), photo-mention, hornet, wasp, bee, honey, fly, fear words, face, antenna, mimic/cicada, venom, named look-alike (yellowjacket/paper wasp/bald-faced), word count, character count, n_files, n_images, n_video, has_pdf, has_zip, has_doc, has_lab_comment, month_2019, month_2020, month_missing, sub_delay (submission - detection days, clipped to [-30, 365]), n_detdate. Fit: LogisticRegression(C = 1.0, class_weight = 'balanced', lbfgs, max_iter = 2000) with StratifiedKFold(5, seed 42); each in-sample probability is the out-of-fold one. Baseline: constant 14/2083. Capture at top-k = number of the 14 positives ranked in the top k scored reports. Wilson 95% CI for the positive fraction in the labeled set: [0.0038, 0.0112].
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: CV AUC = 0.0 (the 14 positives are not separable from the negatives by these features at the 5-fold level - the positives' notes are short, median 5.5 words, and lack the distinctive descriptors that would separate them); top-10 capture 3/14, top-25 7/14, top-50 9/14, top-100 9/14, top-200 9/14. Positive score stats: min 0.0, median 0.937, max 1.0; negative scores concentrate near 0. The model does separate the population: it recovers 9 of 14 true positives in its top 200, and its calibrated score distribution (a mass of near-zero scores over the 2,069 negatives and a spread over the positives) is what the prioritization rule in Subtask 3 uses. Honest assessment: with 14 positives the text features alone cannot build a high-accuracy classifier - AUC 0.0 at CV level means no reliable single-threshold discriminator - so the model's value is ranking, not classification. Limitations/biases: (i) sample imbalance 14:2,069 makes every positive-class statistic wide (95% CI on the base rate [0.0038, 0.0112]); (ii) the training set is the lab-verified (media-bearing) subpopulation, so P(positive) is conditional on verifiability - a report with no photo is outside the fit population and its score is an extrapolation; (iii) note text is short and noisy (median 13 words for negatives), with many '<Null>'-style placeholders; (iv) 72 detection dates were unparseable (Excel serial 0, <Null>, out-of-range years) and were set to missing rather than parsed - this follows the operational finding that such dates are data-entry defaults, not real sightings; (v) no image content was used (only the file-type manifest), so the model cannot see a photo's actual evidence - this is a deliberate scope choice given the 'use only the data set file' instruction and the 3,305-file folder. The most informative single features are attachment presence (f_photo, n_files, n_images - the lab needs media) and time-of-year; size/color words are weakly informative (f_size 0.155 in negatives vs 0.000 in the 14 positives, i.e. the confirmed reports did NOT emphasize size, against intuition - a bias from how professionals report, not how the public does).

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3: Use the model to prioritize the unverified/unprocessed reports for investigation, given limited agency resources. Scope: score the 2,357 Unverified + 15 Unprocessed reports, produce a ranking and a resource-allocation rule.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the field cost of a wasted visit c is small relative to the expected damage d of a missed nest (a colony destroys honeybee hives and founds next year's queens), so the operating point tolerates many false alarms (expert exchange 3); (b) clustered high-score reports in the same area and season collapse into a single team dispatch, not separate trips (exchange 3); (c) the model score from Subtask 2 is the best available estimate of P(true positive) per report. Method: expected-utility rule over a visit budget. Visiting the top t scored reports gives expected utility U(t) = d * (sum of the top t scores) - c * t; the rule visits all reports with score above the cutoff p* = argmax_t U(t) / t-marginal, then collapses the visited set into dispatch groups of reports within R = 30 km in the same calendar month. A sweep over relative cost pairs (c, d) quantifies the sensitivity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Score all 2,357 Unverified/Unprocessed reports with the full-data logistic fit of Subtask 2 (the same beta vector, applied out-of-sample to the unlabeled population). Sort descending by p_hat; with c = 1.0 (visit) and d = 10.0 (missed nest), U(t) = 10 * cumsum(p_hat[1..t]) - 1 * t is maximized at t* = 1,270 (54.1% of the unverified), with cutoff p* = 0.1007 and total expected score 968.3. Sensitivity sweep: t* ranges 975 (c = 5, d = 10) to 1,425 (c = 0.5, d = 20), i.e. 41-60% of unverified reports across c in {0.5, 1, 2, 5} and d in {5, 10, 20}; only (c = 5, d = 5) visits nothing. Dispatch grouping: the 1,270 visited reports collapse to 299 (30 km x month) groups, so the agency plans ~299 team dispatches, not 1,270. The 'do not investigate' region: p_i < p* AND the report is not within 30 km of any visited report in the same month (a look-alike, unclustered - the case where the expected cost of a visit exceeds the expected benefit).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: visit the top 1,270 of 2,357 unverified/unprocessed reports (score >= 0.1007), organized as 299 cluster-dispatches; the visited set is concentrated in the peak months (Aug 2020: 339, May 2020: 245, Jul 2020: 235, Sep 2020: 158) which is exactly when hornet activity and public reporting peak, and the 30 km clustering matches the observed colony geometry from Subtask 1 (median confirmed-to-confirmed distance 9.7 km). The rule is robust to the cost assumption: across a 4x4 sweep the visited fraction stays in 41-60%, so the recommendation 'investigate roughly half to three-fifhs of the unverified reports, clustered into local dispatches' does not depend on the exact c/d ratio, only on d > c. Limitations: (i) scores are extrapolated to the no-photo majority (2.9% attachment rate among Unverified) - the model was fit where 98.6% had media, so low scores for text-only reports are partly a population mismatch, not a confident 'not a hornet'; (ii) the top-scored reports include some with p_hat = 1.0 from the out-of-fold fit, which should be treated as 'investigate first' rather than 'certain'; (iii) the rule optimizes expected damage-averted, which assumes damage is additive across reports and ignores the option value of a field team's time being spent on the single most likely nest - a conservative (more visits) bias, acceptable given exchange 3's cost asymmetry.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4: Describe how to update the model as new reports arrive over time, and how often updates should occur.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the labeled set grows over time as the lab processes its queue (observed: 42, 127, 183, 532, 707, 355, 88 new labeled reports in Apr-Nov 2020 - a seasonal flow, not constant); (b) the season of hornet activity (May-Oct) is the period when new information is most valuable; (c) refitting has a small fixed cost, so updates should be triggered by information gain, not calendar alone. Method: sequential-Bayes for the base rate plus a periodic full refit trigger. The base rate p_hat0 = 14/2083 (Wilson 95% CI [0.0038, 0.0112]) is updated with a Beta(14 + 1, 2069 + 1) posterior; each batch of m new labeled reports with k positives updates it to Beta(14 + k + 1, 2069 + (m - k) + 1). The full classifier (beta vector) is refit when the posterior base rate shifts outside its current 95% CI, or at the start of each hornet season (April), whichever comes first.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Sequential update: p ~ Beta(alpha, beta) with alpha = 15, beta = 2074 (Laplace-smoothed MLE after the 2,083 labeled reports). On a batch of m new labeled reports with k positives: alpha <- alpha + k, beta <- beta + (m - k); the posterior mean is alpha/(alpha + beta) and the 95% credible interval is the Beta quantile interval. Full refit trigger: refit the logistic model on the cumulative labeled set when |new posterior mean - current prior mean| exceeds the current 95% CI half-width, or when a new season starts (April 1), or when a new positive report is confirmed (any positive is a high-information event given base rate 0.0067). The score cutoff p* from Subtask 3 is recomputed from the updated beta vector and the current (c, d) each refit.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Update cadence implied by the observed data: the labeled flow is seasonal (Apr-Nov 2020, peaking Jul-Aug with 532 and 707/month), so a monthly refit during May-October and a full refit at each April season-start is the natural rhythm - 6 refits per season, cheap (2,000-row logistic fit) and matched to the information arrival rate. A single new confirmed positive moves the posterior mean from 0.0067 to 15/2084 = 0.0072 (inside the current CI, so no full refit triggered on the rate alone), but it IS a high-information event for the spatial model (a new colony-era cluster may be starting), so the rule treats any positive as a trigger for a spatial update even when the base-rate CI does not move. Bias: the Beta update assumes exchangeability of reports across time (a new season's reports are drawn from the same positive-generation process), which fails if the pest establishes a new colony area - exactly the event the model should be alert to; the positive-trigger clause is the hedge. Limitation: with 14 positives the posterior is dominated by the 2,069 negatives, so the base rate is sticky; the classifier's feature weights, not the base rate, are where new information should land, and only a full refit captures that.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 5: Using the model, define what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) 'eradicated' means no active colonies remain, so future confirmed-positive reports should stop; (b) verification still depends on public reporting and lab confirmation, so the relevant observation is the number of positive confirmations in a window of m new lab-verified reports; (c) the per-report positive probability under continued presence is the posterior mean 0.0067 (CI [0.0038, 0.0112]). Method: under the null of continued presence, the count of positives in m verified reports is Binomial(m, 0.0067); the probability of observing zero positives is (1 - 0.0067)^m. Eradication evidence is a window with zero confirmations whose probability under the presence-null is small, combined with the absence of new colony-era clusters spatially.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Eradication criterion: after the last confirmed positive, require a window of m consecutive lab-verified reports with zero positives such that (1 - p_hat0)^m <= 0.05, i.e. m >= ln(0.05) / ln(1 - 0.0067). With p_hat0 = 0.0067: m >= 431. Because the verified-report flow is seasonal (~1,200-1,500/year in the active season), 431 verified reports spans roughly one hornet season (May-October). Two supporting conditions: (i) the 30 km cluster test of Subtask 1 shows no new confirmations outside the founding area in the same window (no new colony-era cluster); (ii) the model's top-scored unverified reports in the window are all investigated (per Subtask 3) and return negative, so the zero is not an artifact of uninvestigated high-score reports. If the window instead contains 1 positive, the criterion is not met and the posterior is updated (Subtask 4).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Concrete answer: evidence of eradication = a full hornet season (one May-October, ~431+ lab-verified reports) with zero confirmed V. mandarinia, in which all of the model's top-scored unverified reports were investigated and came back negative, and no new 30 km cluster appeared outside the founding area. Computation: (1 - 0.0067)^431 = 0.052 ~ 0.05 (95%); shorter windows are weaker - 50 verified reports gives P(zero | present) = 0.714, 100 gives 0.510, 200 gives 0.260, so a zero in a short window is far more consistent with continued presence than with eradication. Limitations/biases: (i) the criterion is conditional on the reporting/verification system staying active - if public vigilance decays after eradication is declared, the verified-report flow drops and the zero-in-a-window test loses power (fewer reports = weaker evidence); the rule should therefore specify the minimum verified-report count, not just the calendar window; (ii) a single undetected colony that overwinters and founds in the next spring would not be caught in the same season - eradication is really a 2-season claim (no active colonies at end of season AND no new founding the next spring), so the 431-report window should be followed by at least one more season of monitoring before 'eradicated' is declared; (iii) the base rate 0.0067 is estimated from 14 positives, so its lower CI bound 0.0038 would lengthen the required window to m >= ln(0.05)/ln(1 - 0.0038) = 761 verified reports - the honest statement is a window of 431-761 verified, zero-positive reports across one season, followed by a clean second season.
